title: MLPC 05 - Decision Trees, Random Forests, and SVMs
subject: Machine Learning and Pattern Classification
description: Covers baseline classifiers, ID3, information gain, pruning, random forests, margins, kernels, and support vector machines. All questions are single-choice and modeled after the conceptual style of the MLPC Retry 2024S exam. Source: 05_Common_Machine_Learning_Algorithms.pdf.

questions.question: Which weakness of Naive Bayes follows directly from its independence assumption?

options.text: It cannot handle multiple classes
It may estimate probabilities poorly when features are correlated
It has no training algorithm
It requires a distance metric

questions.explanation: Correlated features violate the conditional-independence assumption and can distort probability estimates.

questions.question: Which statement about k-nearest neighbours is correct?

options.text: Training is expensive but prediction is constant-time
It stores examples and can represent complex boundaries
It is unaffected by irrelevant features
It always produces an interpretable rule set

questions.explanation: k-NN has little explicit training but relies on stored examples and can form flexible boundaries.

questions.question: ID3 chooses a split feature primarily by:

options.text: Maximizing information gain
Minimizing the number of branches regardless of labels
Selecting the first numeric feature
Maximizing training-set size

questions.explanation: Information gain measures the expected reduction in class-label entropy.

questions.question: A node contains examples from only one class. What does ID3 do?

options.text: Splits on every remaining feature
Creates a leaf labeled with that class
Restarts from the root
Uses the global majority class

questions.explanation: A pure node is a stopping case and becomes a leaf.

questions.question: Why is ID3 described as greedy?

options.text: It evaluates every possible complete tree
It selects the locally best split without guaranteeing the globally simplest tree
It always chooses the feature with most values
It removes training examples after each split

questions.explanation: Local information-gain decisions are efficient but can miss globally better combinations.

questions.question: For a numeric feature A, a standard decision-tree split has which form?

options.text: A is a probability
A <= t
A equals every observed value simultaneously
A is removed from all examples

questions.explanation: Numeric features are commonly split using binary threshold tests.

questions.question: What is the intended effect of post-pruning?

options.text: Grow no tree at all
First fit a detailed tree, then remove subtrees that harm validation performance
Increase training accuracy at any cost
Convert the tree into k-NN

questions.explanation: Post-pruning simplifies an already grown tree to improve generalisation.

questions.question: Why can a random forest combine individually overfitting trees successfully?

options.text: All trees make identical errors
Diverse, weakly correlated errors can be reduced by voting
Voting removes the need for data
Every tree is linear

questions.explanation: High-variance trees that overfit differently can produce a stable ensemble prediction.

questions.question: At each random-forest node, the standard lecture algorithm considers:

options.text: Every feature in a fixed order
A random subset of features
Only the target label
No feature because trees are untrained

questions.explanation: Random feature subsets decorrelate the trees and improve the ensemble.

questions.question: Which is a disadvantage of a random forest compared with a single small decision tree?

options.text: It cannot classify new examples
The ensemble is much less interpretable
It is necessarily less robust to noise
It cannot use numeric features

questions.explanation: Combining many trees sacrifices the simple rule-based interpretation of one tree.

questions.question: What does a hard-margin SVM maximize when the training data are linearly separable?

options.text: The number of features
The distance between the separator and the nearest training examples
The empirical class imbalance
The depth of a decision tree

questions.explanation: The maximum-margin hyperplane is as far as possible from the closest points of both classes.

questions.question: Which training examples determine the position of an SVM separator?

options.text: Only examples farthest from the boundary
The support vectors nearest the margin
Only the majority-class examples
All examples with equal influence

questions.explanation: Only support vectors have nonzero influence in the final dual-form classifier.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the soft-margin formulation?

options.text: Require perfect separation in every dataset
Trade margin size against violations or classification errors
Remove the kernel function
Turn binary labels into probabilities

questions.explanation: Slack or hinge-loss terms permit errors when perfect separation is impossible or undesirable.

questions.question: What does the kernel trick avoid?

options.text: Computing class labels
Explicitly constructing the potentially huge transformed feature vectors
Choosing a binary decision
Using dot products

questions.explanation: A kernel computes transformed-space dot products directly from original-space vectors.

questions.question: A circular boundary in the original feature space may become what after a suitable quadratic feature mapping?

options.text: A linear hyperplane in the transformed space
An unlabeled cluster
A decision-tree leaf
A probability that must equal zero

questions.explanation: Nonlinear mappings can make a nonlinear original-space problem linearly separable in a higher-dimensional space.
